input.currentSkills: 3 years running campaigns, some analytics, coordinated with dev on a launch

starting_point.summary: Three years of campaign work, some analytics experience, and direct coordination with a dev team on a launch give you genuine grounding in cross-functional work and data-informed decisions — both commonly relevant to product management. The coordination with dev is particularly transferable because it suggests you have navigated a boundary that many marketing-only backgrounds have not crossed.
starting_point.important_unknown: Product manager roles vary substantially by company — some weight technical depth heavily, others weight go-to-market or customer research; without a specific job posting, the gaps flagged here are based on what is commonly relevant to the role, not what any particular employer requires.

transferable_strengths.evidence: You coordinated with a dev team on a launch.
transferable_strengths.transfer: That experience may carry over to working across engineering and other functions, which is commonly part of a PM role — though the scope and depth of that coordination is not established from what you described.

transferable_strengths.evidence: You have run campaigns for three years.
transferable_strengths.transfer: Running campaigns involves scoping work, sequencing tasks, and delivering to a deadline, which may carry over to managing a product initiative — though PM planning typically includes additional dimensions like tradeoff decisions and engineering constraints.

transferable_strengths.evidence: You have some analytics experience as part of your campaign work.
transferable_strengths.transfer: Familiarity with data as part of decision-making is commonly relevant to product management, though the depth and tools involved are not established from what you described.

transferable_strengths.evidence: Coordinating a launch across marketing and dev implies communicating across different functions with different vocabularies and priorities.
transferable_strengths.transfer: That may carry over to the stakeholder communication a PM regularly handles, though the nature of your coordination — whether you were driving decisions or executing someone else's plan — is not established.

start_here.why_it_matters: Translating user needs and business goals into a prioritized set of requirements is commonly relevant to product management, and it is the capability most distinctly different from marketing coordination work.
start_here.current_evidence: You have written or coordinated around specs in a launch context is not established — your supplied experience covers campaigns, analytics, and launch coordination, but not requirement definition or prioritization decisions.
start_here.gap: Moving from coordinating around a launch to owning the articulation of what gets built, why, and in what order is the core PM capability your supplied experience does not yet demonstrate.
start_here.next_move: Write a one-page requirements doc or prioritized feature brief for a product you use or know well — a concrete artifact you can discuss.
start_here.proof: A written requirements doc or prioritized problem statement that reflects tradeoffs you made and the reasoning behind them.

next_move.primary: Pick a product you use regularly and write a short requirements or prioritization brief for one feature or improvement: describe the user problem, why it matters, what you would build to address it, and what you would leave out and why. Keep it to one page.
next_move.why: This directly builds the capability identified in start_here, and produces a concrete artifact — something you can revise, show, or talk through — without requiring any access or permission you do not already have.
next_move.proof: A written brief that shows you can frame a problem, make a prioritization tradeoff, and articulate a rationale — usable as a starting portfolio piece.
alternatives: If you have access to any product decisions or roadmap discussions in your current role, volunteer to document the problem being solved and the options considered — the same skill applied to real work.
If you can get time with a PM in your network or current company, ask to see how they write requirements or PRDs, then use that as a model for your own practice document.

skill_gaps.target_relevance: PMs commonly need to surface user needs through interviews, usability observation, or other structured methods — not just interpret data after the fact.
skill_gaps.current_evidence: None supplied — your analytics experience may involve interpreting campaign data, but direct user research is not described.
skill_gaps.gap: There is no supplied evidence of conducting discovery conversations, synthesizing qualitative feedback, or translating user input into product direction.
skill_gaps.next_move: Conduct a few informal interviews with people who use a product you know, then write up what you learned and what it implies for the product.
skill_gaps.proof: A short synthesis document — even one page — showing the problem you heard, patterns across conversations, and what they suggest.

skill_gaps.target_relevance: PMs commonly need to make and document prioritization decisions that weigh competing factors — user value, technical cost, business goal — rather than executing a plan handed down.
skill_gaps.current_evidence: Running campaigns and coordinating a launch suggests experience executing against plans, but whether you were making tradeoff decisions or carrying them out is not established.
skill_gaps.gap: Supplied experience does not establish ownership of prioritization decisions or the reasoning behind build-versus-defer tradeoffs.
skill_gaps.next_move: In your practice requirements brief, explicitly document at least two options you considered and why you chose one over the other.
skill_gaps.proof: Written tradeoff reasoning — even in a practice doc — that shows you can weigh competing considerations, not just describe a chosen direction.

skill_gaps.capability: Working with engineering on scope and feasibility
skill_gaps.target_relevance: PMs commonly need to negotiate scope, understand technical constraints at a useful level, and align with engineering on what is feasible within a timeframe.
skill_gaps.current_evidence: You coordinated with dev on a launch — this is relevant, though the nature of that coordination (whether you were discussing scope and feasibility or handling communication logistics) is not established.
skill_gaps.gap: Coordination on a launch does not establish experience negotiating scope, pushing back on estimates, or making build-versus-buy-versus-defer decisions with engineering input.
skill_gaps.next_move: Reflect on your launch coordination and document what decisions were made, who made them, and how — that reflection will clarify what to deepen.
skill_gaps.proof: A written account of a cross-functional decision from that launch, framed from the perspective of what problem was being solved and what tradeoffs were involved.

skill_gaps.target_relevance: PMs commonly own the metrics that define whether a feature or product is succeeding, which is distinct from tracking campaign performance metrics.
skill_gaps.current_evidence: You have some analytics experience, likely in a campaign context — the tools, metrics, and decisions involved are not described.
skill_gaps.gap: Campaign analytics and product analytics serve different questions — defining activation, retention, or adoption metrics for a product feature is not established by campaign measurement experience.
skill_gaps.next_move: For the product in your practice brief, define two or three metrics that would tell you whether your proposed feature is working, and write a sentence on why each one.
skill_gaps.proof: A short metrics section in your practice doc that names success conditions, not just outputs.

skill_gaps.capability: Communicating product strategy to varied audiences
skill_gaps.target_relevance: PMs often need to present direction and rationale to executives, engineering teams, and other stakeholders — each requiring a different framing of the same information.
skill_gaps.current_evidence: Campaign coordination and launch work imply some cross-functional communication, but crafting strategic narratives for different audiences is not established.
skill_gaps.gap: There is no supplied evidence of presenting a product strategy or roadmap direction and adapting the framing to an executive or a skeptical technical audience.
skill_gaps.next_move: Take your practice requirements brief and write a two-paragraph version for a non-technical stakeholder and a separate two-paragraph version for an engineering lead — same content, different framing.
skill_gaps.proof: Two written versions of the same product argument, demonstrating that you can adjust framing without changing the substance.

role_expectations_to_check.question: Whether the target PM role expects ownership of discovery and roadmap decisions, or operates more as a coordination and execution function between stakeholders
role_expectations_to_check.why_it_matters: A coordination-heavy PM role may draw more directly on the visitor's campaign and cross-functional coordination experience, while a discovery-and-strategy-led role would require building skills less evidenced by what they described
role_expectations_to_check.how_to_verify: Read job postings carefully for language like 'define the roadmap' vs. 'partner with stakeholders to deliver' — then talk to someone currently in that type of PM role to hear how the balance plays out day to day

role_expectations_to_check.question: Whether the role requires fluency with quantitative product metrics — retention, activation, funnel analysis — beyond campaign or traffic analytics
role_expectations_to_check.why_it_matters: Marketing analytics and product analytics overlap in tooling but differ in what is being measured and why; if the role expects the visitor to own instrumentation decisions or interpret behavioral data, the gap may be larger than 'some analytics' alone establishes
role_expectations_to_check.how_to_verify: Look for phrases like 'define success metrics,' 'work with data science,' or specific tools named in postings for roles at companies you are targeting

role_expectations_to_check.question: Whether the role expects prior PM title and experience, or is open to adjacent-background candidates making a deliberate transition
role_expectations_to_check.why_it_matters: Some PM openings screen for prior PM title as a baseline, which would make this a harder door to push through directly; others hire for demonstrated product thinking from adjacent roles, which is a more navigable path given the visitor's background
role_expectations_to_check.how_to_verify: Check the 'required' vs. 'preferred' sections of postings carefully, and look for roles labeled 'associate PM,' 'growth PM,' or 'technical program manager' that may serve as stepping-stone entry points

role_expectations_to_check.question: Whether the role sits in a domain where the visitor's marketing background is relevant — growth, acquisition, consumer product — vs. a domain where it is largely orthogonal
role_expectations_to_check.why_it_matters: A PM role on a growth or marketing product team could treat the visitor's campaign and analytics background as a genuine asset; a role in infrastructure, platform, or B2B enterprise product would not
role_expectations_to_check.how_to_verify: Look at the product area described in each posting and ask whether someone with no marketing background would be disadvantaged there — if not, the domain fit argument weakens

transition_tasks.task: Reframe the dev-launch coordination and campaign work on the resume using product language — problem, decision, outcome — rather than marketing execution language
transition_tasks.why: Hiring managers reading for PM fit will look for evidence of ownership and judgment; the same experience described in campaign terms reads differently than described in terms of what was decided and what changed as a result

transition_tasks.task: Identify and reach out to people currently working as PMs who came from marketing, coordination, or other non-engineering backgrounds
transition_tasks.why: This transition is common enough that people have navigated it recently; firsthand accounts of which roles, companies, or entry points were accessible will be more accurate than any general pattern

transition_tasks.task: Find and apply to roles where the marketing-to-product path is a recognized fit — growth PM, consumer PM, or PM roles explicitly tied to acquisition or lifecycle — rather than applying broadly
transition_tasks.why: Targeting roles where the visitor's background is a plausible asset, rather than a gap to explain away, changes the strength of the application before any skill-building occurs

unknowns: Whether the dev coordination experience involved the visitor making or influencing product decisions, or was primarily logistical handoff work — this distinction materially affects how much of that experience is transferable as PM evidence
What industry or product domain the visitor is targeting, which affects both which PM roles are reachable and whether the marketing background reads as relevant or unrelated

Whether the visitor has any artifacts — a brief, a spec, a launch retrospective, a dashboard they built — that could demonstrate product-adjacent thinking concretely, or whether the transition argument rests entirely on job title and description

input.currentRole: Software engineer, 5 years backend Python/APIs. No management experience.
input.currentSkills: Backend Python and API architecture, system design, wrote specs, cross-functional collaboration with product and design, ran one user interview, comfortable with SQL
input.interests: User research, strategy and business impact

directions.why_it_connects: You supplied experience writing specs, collaborating cross-functionally with product and design, and a stated interest in strategy and business impact — these are directly relevant to how product management work is commonly described.
directions.what_the_work_involves: Product managers commonly define what gets built and why, working across engineering, design, and business stakeholders to shape roadmaps and decisions. The balance between technical depth, user understanding, and business framing varies considerably by organization and product type.
directions.worth_learning_more_about: Would you want to make decisions about what gets built without being the one who builds it — and would you find the influence-without-authority dynamic of the role satisfying day to day?
directions.one_way_to_investigate: Read first-person accounts from engineers who moved into product management — search for these on personal blogs or LinkedIn posts — and look at a range of product manager job postings to see how much technical depth different organizations expect.

directions.why_it_connects: You stated an interest in user research and supplied that you ran a user interview, which gives you at least some direct exposure to the practice.
directions.what_the_work_involves: UX researchers plan and conduct studies — interviews, usability tests, surveys — to understand how people think about and use products, then synthesize findings to inform design and product decisions. The scope and methods used vary considerably by team size and maturity.
directions.worth_learning_more_about: Would you want to spend a large portion of your time in the study-design and synthesis cycle, rather than in building systems — and does the pace of research-driven work match what you are looking for?
directions.one_way_to_investigate: Look for job postings for UX researcher roles and note what methods and deliverables they list, then find first-person writing from researchers about what a typical project actually looks like week to week.

directions.target_role: Developer tools or API strategy role
directions.why_it_connects: You supplied five years of backend Python and API architecture work, which is directly relevant to work focused on developer-facing products or API strategy — areas where deep technical context shapes the work.
directions.what_the_work_involves: Some organizations have roles — sometimes called developer advocate, developer experience, or technical product roles — focused on shaping or communicating APIs and tools for external or internal developers. The mix of writing, research, strategy, and building varies widely by organization.
directions.worth_learning_more_about: Would you want your technical background to remain central to your day-to-day work, or are you looking to move toward roles where it is more of a background asset than the primary focus?
directions.one_way_to_investigate: Search job postings for 'developer experience,' 'API product,' and 'developer advocate' to see the range of what these roles involve, and look for first-person accounts from people in them about where they spend their time.

directions.why_it_connects: You stated an interest in strategy and business impact, and supplied experience with SQL and cross-functional collaboration — capabilities that are commonly relevant to strategy and operations work that involves data and stakeholder coordination.
directions.what_the_work_involves: Strategy and operations roles commonly involve analyzing data, framing business problems, and working across teams to drive decisions or improvements. These roles exist in many forms — inside product companies, consulting, or business operations — and the technical depth expected varies considerably.
directions.worth_learning_more_about: Would you want to work primarily on business and organizational problems rather than product or user problems — and does the idea of influencing decisions through analysis and communication, rather than through building, appeal to you?
directions.one_way_to_investigate: Look at job postings for 'strategy and operations,' 'business operations analyst,' and 'go-to-market strategy' roles at companies whose products interest you, and compare what each actually lists as day-to-day responsibilities.

current_salary_range.note: Higher end requires 4+ years experience or a mid-size market; entry-level coordinators in smaller metros often land at $42–48K.

target_salary_range.note: Entry-level PM salaries cluster near $70–80K outside FAANG; startup PMs may earn less cash but receive equity that could be worthless.

salary_delta.realistic_starting_salary: A career-changer landing their first PM role in 2026 without a CS background or MBA should realistically target $68–75K, not the $82K midpoint, especially at companies below 500 employees.

transition_costs.item: Product management certificate (e.g., Product School, Reforge, or Pragmatic Institute)
transition_costs.note: Not a hiring requirement at most companies, but signals commitment to interviewers who will otherwise question why a marketer can handle roadmapping and technical scoping.

transition_costs.item: Books and self-study materials (Inspired, Shape Up, Continuous Discovery Habits, etc.)
transition_costs.note: Interview loops for PM roles test product sense and frameworks directly; showing up without this knowledge is disqualifying.

transition_costs.item: Side project or portfolio work (domain hosting, tools, design software subscriptions)
transition_costs.note: Hiring managers expect a portfolio or case study since you lack shipped-product experience; this signals initiative and gives interview material.

transition_costs.item: Networking and informational interviews (travel, coffee meetings, LinkedIn Premium ~6 months)
transition_costs.note: Most PM hires happen through warm referrals, not cold applications; this is not optional if you want a 6-month timeline to be realistic.

transition_costs.item: Income gap during active job search (assumes 2–3 months of reduced freelance/part-time work to interview)
transition_costs.note: PM interview processes average 4–8 weeks per company and often require take-home assignments; most candidates reduce work hours and absorb the income hit.
Useful if you have no internal advocate to review PM-specific framing of your marketing experience.

roi_analysis.year_3_cumulative: Assuming a $20K annual raise held and modest PM progression, you recoup transition costs in roughly 6 months and net approximately $51K more over 3 years after subtracting the $9,350 in costs.
roi_analysis.year_5_cumulative: If you earn one promotion to mid-level PM by year 3 (realistic), cumulative earnings advantage over staying in marketing reaches approximately $120–140K over 5 years.

output.negotiation_leverage: Your marketing background is genuinely differentiable — most PMs lack fluency in user messaging, go-to-market coordination, and campaign analytics, so lean hard on that in B2C or growth-focused roles where those skills directly map to PM responsibilities.
output.financial_warning: The 6-month timeline is aggressive for a career-changer with no shipped product experience; if the search stretches to 10–12 months (which is common), the income gap cost nearly doubles and payback period extends past year 1 — plan your cash reserves accordingly.

skillGaps.capability: Working with engineering on scope and feasibility
Communicating product strategy to varied audiences

first.focus: Start with user research and discovery, because it is the foundation the other gaps build on — structuring tradeoffs and defining metrics both require knowing what you learned from users and why it matters. Your marketing background gives you real exposure to audiences and messaging, which overlaps with research thinking.
first.how_youll_know: You can take a specific product or feature you already know well, write down three distinct user problems it might solve, and then explain — in plain language, without marketing framing — which one you would prioritize investigating first and why the others can wait.

then.focus: Move to structuring product decisions with tradeoffs, using what you learned in the first phase as your raw material — practice making a real or realistic decision where you have to weigh user needs against constraints you name explicitly.

later.focus: Working with engineering on scope and feasibility, and defining and tracking product metrics, can develop in parallel once the earlier two are underway — both benefit from having a concrete decision-making framework in place first. Communicating product strategy is a useful gap to address through the work itself: practice explaining decisions you have already made in the earlier phases to someone outside product.

output.plateau_note: The fix when you feel stuck: find or create one small, low-stakes product problem you can own all the way through, even outside a formal job context.
